Vizsoly Bible
viz'-oly bī'-bl
n. (the Vizsoly Bible, 1590, the first complete Hungarian Bible, printed at Vizsoly in Zemplen)
Vizsoly, the village in north-eastern Hungary where the press stood; Greek biblia, books.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Vizsoly Bible is the first complete Bible in Hungarian, translated chiefly by Gaspar Karoli with a team of fellow pastors and printed at Vizsoly in the county of Zemplen between February 1589 and July 1590. The press was set up for the purpose in a village of a few hundred souls, under the protection of Sigismund Rakoczi, and worked by Balint Mantskovit; about eight hundred copies were printed in two folio volumes, of which some fifty survive. It came to a church already confessionally settled under Melius but without the whole of Scripture in its own tongue, and it arrived just before the Counter-Reformation closed in: for the next two centuries Hungarian Reformed families held worship around this book while their colleges were suppressed and their pastors sent to the galleys. Revised by Albert Molnar in 1608 and many times since, it remains the Hungarian Authorized Version. “Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee” (Psa 119:11) describes exactly what the Magyar households did with it, there being for long stretches nowhere else to keep it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the Bible as the volume which contains the Scriptures, and a folio as a book of the largest size, formed by once doubling a sheet.

BI'BLE, n. The Book by way of eminence; the sacred volume.

FO'LIO, n. A book of the largest size, formed by once doubling a sheet of paper.

PRESS, n. An instrument or machine by which any body is squeezed; a printing machine.

Modern Corruption

The first complete Hungarian Bible, eight hundred copies from a village press in 1590.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. It is worth noticing what the Vizsoly Bible cost and what it bought. A village press, a patron's protection, two years, eight hundred copies — and with that a church survived two centuries of suppression with no seminary, often no pastor, and no legal standing.

The principle to recover is that faith comes by hearing the word and nothing else will serve as a substitute: “So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17). Where preaching was forbidden, the household reading of this book was the hearing; and a child so taught “hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation” (2Ti 3:15).
